name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ISOLATIONOFELEMENTS_MCQ_Q01 - Extraction of iron in blast furnace and copper matte

questiontext.text:
Consider the following statements regarding the extraction of iron and copper from their ores:

  1. In the blast furnace, within the \(500\text{–}800\,\mathrm{K}\) temperature range, \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}\) and \(\mathrm{FeO}\) by \(\mathrm{CO}\), while limestone decomposes to \(\mathrm{CaO}\) to remove silicate impurities as molten \(\mathrm{CaSiO_3}\) slag.
  2. Cast iron is the purest form of commercial iron, obtained from pig iron by oxidising impurities in a reverberatory furnace lined with haematite.
  3. When iron-containing sulphide ores of copper are heated with silica in a reverberatory furnace, iron oxide forms \(\mathrm{FeSiO_3}\) slag and copper is obtained as copper matte containing \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\) and \(\mathrm{FeS}\).
  4. When copper matte is treated with a hot air blast in a silica-lined converter, the solidified copper obtained is called blister copper due to the evolution of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) gas.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle — Reduction and Slag Formation in the Blast Furnace
In the upper region of the blast furnace (\(500\text{–}800\,\mathrm{K}\)), iron(III) oxide is reduced stepwise by carbon monoxide: \(3\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + \mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe_3O_4} + \mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + \mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{CO_2}\). Simultaneously, limestone (\(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\)) decomposes to \(\mathrm{CaO}\), which acts as a basic flux and combines with acidic silica (\(\mathrm{SiO_2}\)) gangue to form molten calcium silicate (\(\mathrm{CaSiO_3}\)) slag. Thus, the proposition describing blast furnace reactions and slag formation is correct.

Step 2: Conceptual Evaluation — Distinction Between Cast Iron and Wrought Iron
Pig iron from the blast furnace contains about \(4\%\) carbon. Melting pig iron with scrap iron and coke using a hot air blast produces cast iron, which has about \(3\%\) carbon and is extremely hard and brittle. The purest form of commercial iron is wrought iron (malleable iron), which is prepared from cast iron—not pig iron—by oxidising carbon and other impurities in a reverberatory furnace lined with haematite (\(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + 3\mathrm{C} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + 3\mathrm{CO}\)). Therefore, the proposition identifying cast iron as the purest commercial form prepared in a haematite-lined furnace is incorrect.

Step 3: Conceptual Application — Copper Matte Formation
In the reverberatory furnace, copper sulphide ores containing iron are mixed with silica and heated. Iron(II) oxide reacts with silica to slag off as iron silicate (\(\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{FeSiO_3}\)), leaving behind copper matte, a molten mixture of \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\) and \(\mathrm{FeS}\). Hence, the proposition describing copper matte and \(\mathrm{FeSiO_3}\) slag formation is correct.

Step 4: Conceptual Application — Formation of Blister Copper
In a silica-lined converter, hot air oxidises remaining \(\mathrm{FeS}\) and partially converts \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu_2O}\), which then undergoes self-reduction: \(2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} \rightarrow 6\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2}\). As the molten copper cools and solidifies, escaping \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) gas produces blisters on the surface, giving blister copper. Thus, the proposition explaining blister copper is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The propositions concerning blast furnace reduction with \(\mathrm{CaSiO_3}\) slag formation, copper matte formation with \(\mathrm{FeSiO_3}\) slag, and blister copper formation by \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) evolution are correct, whereas the proposition attributing the properties of wrought iron to cast iron is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ISOLATIONOFELEMENTS_MCQ_Q02 - Leaching of bauxite gold cyanide and refining

questiontext.text:
Consider the following statements regarding leaching and refining processes in metallurgy:

  1. During the leaching of bauxite with concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) at \(473\text{–}523\,\mathrm{K}\), both \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) and \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) dissolve to form sodium aluminate and sodium silicate respectively, and passing \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) gas selectively precipitates hydrated \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) while leaving sodium silicate in solution.
  2. In the extraction of gold and silver by cyanide leaching, the metal is first reduced to \([\mathrm{M(CN)_2}]^-\) in an oxygen-free environment, and is later recovered by oxidation using zinc.
  3. In the electrolytic refining of blister copper, impure copper acts as the cathode, pure copper strip acts as the anode, and noble metals such as silver, gold, and platinum dissolve into the acidified \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\) electrolyte.
  4. In the van Arkel method for refining zirconium or titanium, the crude metal is heated with iodine in an evacuated vessel to form a volatile metal iodide, which is decomposed on a tungsten filament heated to about \(1800\,\mathrm{K}\).

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Evaluation — Leaching of Alumina from Bauxite
When powdered bauxite is digested with concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) at \(473\text{–}523\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(35\text{–}36\,\mathrm{bar}\), \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) dissolves as sodium aluminate (\(\mathrm{NaAl(OH)_4}\)) and the \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) impurity dissolves as sodium silicate, while iron oxides and \(\mathrm{TiO_2}\) remain insoluble. Neutralising the filtrate with \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) gas (aided by seeding) precipitates hydrated alumina (\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\cdot x\mathrm{H_2O}\)) while sodium silicate stays in solution. Thus, the proposition describing bauxite leaching is correct.

Step 2: Conceptual Evaluation — Cyanide Leaching of Gold and Silver
In the metallurgy of gold and silver, leaching with dilute \(\mathrm{NaCN}\) or \(\mathrm{KCN}\) requires air (oxygen) to oxidise the native metal (\(\mathrm{M} \rightarrow \mathrm{M^+}\)) into the soluble complex \([\mathrm{M(CN)_2}]^-\): \(4\mathrm{M(s)} + 8\mathrm{CN^-(aq)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow 4[\mathrm{M(CN)_2}]^-\mathrm{(aq)} + 4\mathrm{OH^-(aq)}\). Subsequently, zinc acts as a reducing agent to displace the precious metal: \(2[\mathrm{M(CN)_2}]^-\mathrm{(aq)} + \mathrm{Zn(s)} \rightarrow [\mathrm{Zn(CN)_4}]^{2-}\mathrm{(aq)} + 2\mathrm{M(s)}\). Claiming that the metal is reduced in an oxygen-free environment and recovered by oxidation is incorrect.

Step 3: Conceptual Evaluation — Electrolytic Refining of Copper
During electrolytic refining of blister copper, the impure copper block is made the anode (where \(\mathrm{Cu} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{e^-}\)) and a pure copper strip is made the cathode (where \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}\)). Less basic (noble) impurities such as antimony, selenium, tellurium, silver, gold, and platinum do not dissolve into the electrolyte; instead, they settle below the anode as anode mud. Reversing the electrodes and claiming noble metals dissolve into the electrolyte makes this proposition incorrect.

Step 4: Conceptual Application — Vapour Phase Refining by van Arkel Method
The van Arkel method removes oxygen and nitrogen impurities from zirconium or titanium by heating the crude metal with iodine in an evacuated vessel to form volatile covalent \(\mathrm{ZrI_4}\) (or \(\mathrm{TiI_4}\)). The volatile iodide is then decomposed on an electrically heated tungsten filament at about \(1800\,\mathrm{K}\) to deposit ultra-pure metal (\(\mathrm{ZrI_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zr} + 2\mathrm{I_2}\)). Thus, the proposition describing the van Arkel method is correct.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Only the propositions describing the leaching of bauxite with \(\mathrm{NaOH}/\mathrm{CO_2}\) and the van Arkel refining of zirconium or titanium are scientifically accurate, whereas the propositions describing cyanide leaching and electrolytic refining of copper contain fundamental conceptual errors.
